title: Everyone gets a place (Joshua 13–19)
hook: long lists of borders give every tribe its portion

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sun over Gibeon, told to stand still. Your line was hush, not yet. Did you stop the clock for a few breaths? Today, the chapters it's easy to skim, and why they matter. Day seven hundred six.

The border goes up by a valley. It passes along to a spring of water. It turns toward a mountain, bends around, goes down to the sea. Then a list of towns, name after name after name, with their villages. Then the next tribe, and the next. For several chapters the book of Joshua reads like a surveyor's notebook. It's tempting to skip ahead to the next story. But every one of those names was somebody's front door, somebody's well, somebody's field. These chapters are where the wandering ends, and people get an address.
screen: `THE BORDER GOES UP, TURNS, GOES DOWN.` → `NAME AFTER NAME.` → `SOMEBODY'S FRONT DOOR.`

segments.voice: The text says the portions are given by lot. Nobody gets to grab the best valley; the land is shared out tribe by tribe, family by family. And each portion is named. Inside the lists there are moments. Five sisters, Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah and Tirzah, the daughters of Zelophehad, come before Eleazar the priest and Joshua. Their father had no sons. The Lord commanded Moses, they say, to give us a portion among our brothers. And they receive it, written into the borders with everyone else. A family that could have been left off the map is on it. Then the tribes of Joseph complain that their share is too small and the hill country too crowded. Joshua's answer: there's forest up there; go clear it, and it's yours. Room can be made. And one tribe gets no territory at all. Levi, the tribe of the priests and Levites, receives towns to live in among the others, but no portion of land, because, the text says, the Lord, the God of Israel, is their inheritance. Their place is a calling. A psalm uses the language of these chapters: lines, lots, portions. It sounds like someone looking at their own small share of the world and finding it enough: "The lines are fallen unto me in pleasant places; yea, I have a goodly heritage." The Hebrew for lines is chavalim, and it's the word the book of Joshua uses when shares of land fall to the tribe of Manasseh, in the same chapter as the five sisters. Everyone gets a place, and a place can be a field, a hillside you clear yourself, or a calling.
screen: `GIVEN BY LOT, NAMED BY NAME.` · `ZELOPHEHAD'S DAUGHTERS ON THE MAP.` · `CLEAR THE FOREST: ROOM IS MADE.` · `LEVI: GOD IS THEIR PORTION.` · then, large: `THE LINES ARE FALLEN IN PLEASANT PLACES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: appreciate the place you have. Settle, and look around. This room, this chair, this street, this small piece of the world that is, for now, yours. It may not be the place you'd choose. Notice three things about it anyway: one thing you can see, one thing you can hear, one thing it gives you. Then think of the people who share your lines with you, at home, at work, next door. If you pray, you can hold the psalm's words: the lines are fallen unto me in pleasant places. The bell holds the time.
Everyone gets a place. The border lists of Joshua, where every tribe is given its portion by lot, five daughters claim theirs, and Levi's portion is God. Today's word.
Your line: everyone gets a place. Today, make room for someone: a seat at the table, a turn to speak, a name on the list. Day seven hundred six.

howItsDone: Jews read the border lists of Joshua 13–19 as part of studying the Former Prophets, and the daughters of Zelophehad, whose claim is told in Numbers and completed in Joshua, are studied as a model of asking for justice.

fork.setup: you're one of Zelophehad's daughters. your father died with no sons, and the land is being shared out by family. what do you do?
options: accept that the land will pass you by.
go to the priest and Joshua and claim what Moses promised.
wait until someone thinks of you.
fork.reveal: they stand before Eleazar and Joshua and say: Moses was commanded to give us a portion. and they receive it, among their kin.

original.note: Hebrew: an inheritance, a portion of land held by a family.

trapdoor: what you thought: chapters of boring border lists.
what it means: every tribe gets a place by lot and by name, five daughters claim theirs, and Levi's portion is God.
what a scholar hears: the lines that fell in Psalm 16 are chavalim, the word for the shares that fell to Manasseh in Joshua 17:5.

sources.quoted: The lines are fallen unto me in pleasant places; yea, I have a goodly heritage.

notes: Verify JPS 1917 wording of Psalm 16:6 (certain in the KJV; confirm JPS matches).
'Five sisters' and their names are from Joshua 17:3; the count is in the text.
Chavalim as 'lines' / 'parts' rests on Psalm 16:6 and Joshua 17:5 both using the word with 'fall'; a Keeper may still cut it under the strict etymology rule.
Levi's towns (Joshua 21) are mentioned without a count.
Caleb's portion (14:6–15) is left for tomorrow.

Editor: Zelophehad's daughters now speak their words in 17:4 (the narrator, not they, says their father had no sons); 'the lists are careful because each portion has to be named to be real' cut; Levi called the tribe of the priests and Levites; the chavalim gloss now rests on the text: Joshua 17:5 says shares 'fell' to Manasseh, the word Psalm 16:6 uses.

Audit: the teach said chavalim is 'the word Joshua uses', but Joshua 17:5 is the narrator, not Joshua speaking; now 'the word the book of Joshua uses'. Stale note about 'measuring cords' (no longer in the script) replaced.
